extracted.intended_audience: judges, jurors, and litigators in patent infringement trials (IP litigators and trial courts)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions and legal standards for determining reasonable royalty patent damages, including apportionment rules, comparable-license analysis, the entire-market-value rule, and FRAND considerations. Designed to guide juries (and judges/litigators) in calculating damages consistent with Federal Circuit precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard for damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent holder must prove each element of its damages claim, including the amount of damages, by a 'preponderance of the evidence.' Damages must be adequate to compensate the patent holder and put it in approximately the same financial position it would have been in absent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages need not be proven with mathematical precision but must be shown with reasonable certainty. Damages must compensate, not punish; the jury may not add anything to penalize the infringer or to set an example. (Authorities: 35 U.S.C. §284; Lucent; Aro; Riles; Ericsson v. D-Link.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and timing of hypothetical negotiation (reasonable royalty)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the amount the patent holder and accused infringer would have agreed to immediately before the relevant event (non-SEP: 'pre-investment negotiation'; SEP: 'pre-standard negotiation'). The jury's task is to judge what that outcome would have been.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering the negotiation, focus on what the parties would have known and expected immediately before the negotiation date. If parties contest the negotiation date, the jury must decide it. Evidence of events after that date (ex post evidence) may be considered only to the extent it aids in assessing what the parties would have expected on the earlier date. Assume for the hypothetical negotiation that the parties believed the patent was valid and infringed, were willing to enter an agreement, and would have acted reasonably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 1: Royalty may not exceed incremental value of claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasonable royalty may not exceed the incremental value that the claimed invention contributes to the accused product (and in SEP cases to the relevant standard) compared to the best available alternative to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an overarching cap: royalty must be based on the additional value the claimed invention adds over the best non-infringing alternative. (See also Factor One guidance and authorities like Ericsson, Commc'wlth Sci. & Indus. Research Org. v. Cisco.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 2: Exclude value from non-claimed factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasonable royalty may not include the value that factors other than the claimed invention contribute to the accused product or standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude value added by manufacturing processes, product marketing, brand recognition, and technologies not part of the patented invention (including other patents). Jury should apportion the product's value so the award reflects only the incremental value contributed by the patent-in-suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle 3: Use of comparable license agreements as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparable license agreements, such as those covering use of the claimed invention or similar technology, often indicate the market value of the claimed invention and may be considered in setting a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To use prior agreements as evidence, the offering party must show they are technologically and economically comparable to the hypothetical license at the relevant time. Licenses need not be identical but must be more than loosely comparable. Non-litigation licenses are generally more reliable than settlement agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor One — Incremental value contributed by the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent holder is entitled to recover damages not greater than the cost to the accused infringer of its best alternative to the claimed invention at the negotiation time, plus the value of any additional benefit the claimed invention contributes over that best alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining incremental value requires a baseline: consider whether a commercially acceptable non-infringing alternative was available at the time. If a non-infringing alternative existed, the royalty cannot exceed the invention's incremental value over that alternative. Do not include 'switching costs' (e.g., redesign, retooling, inventory elimination) because the hypothetical negotiation is before the infringer invested in the technology. Authorities: Garretson; Minco; Ericsson; Microsoft v. Motorola; AstraZeneca.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor Two — Value contributed by factors other than the claimed invention (apportionment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasonable royalty should be based solely on the incremental value of the patented invention in the accused products compared to the next best alternative and should not include value added by other factors (manufacturing, marketing, brand, other technologies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury must apportion the value of the infringing product so that the award reflects only the incremental value contributed by the patent(s)-in-suit. Where the claimed invention covers one feature, damages generally must be based at most on the 'smallest saleable unit' that substantially embodies the claimed invention (example: windshield wiper vs. whole car). The cost of the smallest saleable unit generally sets the upper limit on the damages base; further apportionment of that unit may be necessary to isolate the claimed invention's contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire Market Value Rule (EMVR) — narrow application
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire market value rule allows a patentee, in rare circumstances, to recover a royalty based on the value of an entire multi-feature product even when the asserted patent covers only one feature or technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EMVR applies only if the patentee proves the claimed invention is the sole basis driving customer demand for the entire product (or, if modified, that the novel elements in the asserted claim are the sole basis driving demand). If the patentee cannot make that proof, damages must be based on the smallest saleable unit. Authorities: VirnetX; Uniloc; Lucent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor Three — Use and admissibility of comparable agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior license agreements by the patent holder, accused infringer, or third parties for similar technology may be considered if technologically and economically comparable to the hypothetical license at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proponent bears the burden to show comparability by comparing scope, context, and value of the prior agreement to the hypothetical license. Actual contemporaneous licenses can be highly probative. Litigation settlement agreements are disfavored because they may reflect litigation considerations unrelated to incremental value. The court/jury should discount licenses entered after the infringer invested or after standard adoption to the extent they reflect lock-in or ex post factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparability factors to evaluate prior licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding whether a license agreement is technologically and economically comparable, consider multiple dimensions of similarity between the prior license and the hypothetical license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of factors provided: (1) similarity of negotiating circumstances (arms-length, no litigation threat); (2) similarity of license structure to hypothetical license; (3) similarity of patents covered; (4) similarity of products covered; (5) whether other product features/technologies affect comparability; (6) whether other relationships or consideration exchanged affected terms; (7) similarity of relationship between the parties; (8) timing of the agreement relative to when the licensee adopted the technology or standard (post-adoption may reflect lock-in and should be adjusted); (9) whether market circumstances at license time differ from the hypothetical negotiation time. Also: if a license bases royalty on an entire multi-component product, the jury should admit it only if comparable and must apportion out value not attributable to the claimed invention. Authorities: Apple v. Motorola; Ericsson; LaserDynamics; ResQNet; Finjan; Lucent; Wordtech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of ex post evidence and lock-in effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of things that happened after the date of the hypothetical negotiation can be considered only to the extent that such evidence aids in assessing what the parties would have thought or expected on the earlier date; jurors should be instructed to consider whether and how ex post factors such as lock-in costs might have affected license prices or willingness to negotiate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury instruction should focus on the probative value of prior licenses and commercial evidence indicating ex ante willingness to license, while guarding against awarding royalties influenced by ex post opportunistic effects (e.g., lock-in, litigation risk).

rubrics_metrics.name: FRAND-specific adjustments and instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent holder is under a FRAND (Fair, Reasonable, and Non-Discriminatory) obligation, the jury must ensure any damages award is consistent with and does not exceed amounts permitted under the FRAND obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional FRAND-specific guidance appears in alternative Factor Four and discussions of SEP cases: e.g., reasonable royalties for SEPs must not include value flowing from the standard's adoption; courts should consider the patentee's actual RAND commitment when crafting instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catch-all: Consider other relevant factors
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining a reasonable royalty, jurors may also consider any other factors which, in their minds, would have increased or decreased the royalty that the parties would have negotiated at the hypothetical time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits consideration of additional context-specific evidence beyond the enumerated factors, provided it is used to approximate what a willing licensor and licensee would have agreed to immediately before the negotiation event.
